method: A CHOKEPOINTS estimate for 2025. The United States column is anchored on SIA and BCG's measurement of EDA and core IP together, which was 74 percent American and 20 percent European in 2019 (2021 report, Exhibit 14) and 68 and 25 in 2022 (2024 report, Exhibit 2); the EDA-only split is then set by the two American vendors' filed revenue, $4.37bn of EDA product-group revenue at Synopsys in FY2025 (62.0 percent of $7,054.2m) and $3.71bn of Core EDA at Cadence (70 percent of $5,296.8m).
note: Firm shares converted to country by parent-company headquarters. Synopsys (US, $7,054.2m total revenue FY2025, of which the EDA product group was 62.0 percent, Design IP 24.8 and the newly acquired Ansys 10.7) and Cadence (US, $5,296.8m FY2025, of which Core EDA was 70 percent) hold roughly seven-tenths of the EDA tool revenue the row counts; Keysight EDA and PDF Solutions add to the US column. The single largest judgment call is Siemens EDA, the former Mentor Graphics: it is run from Wilsonville, Oregon but owned by Siemens AG, so it is assigned to DE, consistent with the Zeiss=DE convention. Assigning it to the US instead would put the US near 87 percent and drop DE to about 1. Siemens does not disclose EDA revenue separately in its annual report, which makes the German column the least certain number in the row and is why the row is an estimate. JP is Zuken plus Altium, which Renesas acquired in 2024. CN is Empyrean, Primarius, Semitronix and X-Epic, still concentrated in analog and packaging tools, short of a full digital flow. Excludes design IP, which is carried separately under Core IP. CSET's own 2019 figure, carried as node N84 in ETO's provision table, is the United States at 96 percent, because CSET assigns Mentor Graphics to the US.
trend: Static concentration since 2021, except that China's share roughly tripled off a tiny base after the 2025 US export-license episode pushed domestic buyers toward Empyrean and its peers.

method: A CHOKEPOINTS estimate for 2025, built from the design-IP licensing and royalty revenue the largest vendors file (Arm $4,920m in the year to March 2026, Synopsys $1,752m of Design IP in FY2025, Cadence about $742m, or 14 percent of revenue) and moved on from CSET's 2019 split of the segment, carried as node N85 in ETO's provision table, which was US 52, GB 43, CN 2, TW 1 on a $3.9bn market. The denominator is an estimate: Imagination, SiFive and the Chinese houses publish nothing comparable.
note: GB is Arm (Cambridge, revenue $4,920m in the year to March 2026, of which royalties were $2,613m); Other is Imagination Technologies and smaller vendors. Arm is majority-owned by SoftBank of Japan, so a cut by ownership would move those 48 points from GB to JP. US is Synopsys IP, Cadence IP, Rambus, SiFive and Ceva; Alphawave moves from GB to the US column with Qualcomm's acquisition, announced in 2025. CN is VeriSilicon and the domestic RISC-V houses. TW is eMemory. Shares are of design-IP licensing and royalty revenue, with no count of chips shipped using the IP, and the row is an estimate because the four vendors that file cover about four-fifths of it and the rest is private.
trend: Broadly stable UK-US duopoly since 2021, with RISC-V eroding Arm's position at the margin and Chinese IP vendors growing from about 2 percent to about 5 percent.

method: Country shares of the silicon wafer market published by Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry in December 2025, from Fuji Keizai's semiconductor materials survey, on a headquarters basis. Japan's 53 percent is printed on the chart; the other columns are measured off the chart's vector geometry, which reproduces every printed label on the slide exactly and sums to 100.
note: Polished and epitaxial silicon wafers for semiconductor use, by revenue and by parent-company headquarters. JP is Shin-Etsu Handotai and SUMCO; TW is GlobalWafers; KR is SK Siltron; DE is Siltronic, and carries the source's whole European column, which also contains Finland's Okmetic, owned by China's National Silicon Industry Group. There is no meaningful US-headquartered merchant wafer supplier, which is why US is zero even though Shin-Etsu, SUMCO, Siltronic and GlobalWafers all operate US plants. The source publishes no China column at either 2021 or 2023, so Zing Semiconductor, NSIG, Simgui, TCL Zhonghuan and Gritek sit inside the five-point Other column; CSET put China under 5 percent of wafers in 2019, and under 1 percent of 300 mm wafers. The 2019 CSET split, carried as node N26 in ETO's provision table, was JP 56, TW 16, DE 14, KR 10, CN 4 on a $10.9bn market, so the movement since is Japanese and German share going to Taiwan and Korea.
trend: Almost flat on this measure between the source's two cuts: Japan 52.4 percent in 2021 against 53.0 in 2023, Taiwan 19.0 in both, Korea 13.1 against 13.0, Europe 10.3 against 10.0. The movement is at the mature diameters and inside the Other column, where the Chinese 300 mm entrants sit; CSET had China under 5 percent in 2019 and under 1 percent of 300 mm wafers.

method: Country shares of the photoresist market published by Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry in December 2025, from Fuji Keizai's semiconductor materials survey, on a headquarters basis. Japan's 78 percent is printed on the chart; the other columns are measured off the chart's vector geometry, which reproduces every printed label on the slide exactly and sums to 100.
note: Five Japanese firms, JSR, Tokyo Ohka Kogyo, Shin-Etsu Chemical, Sumitomo Chemical and Fujifilm, hold about four-fifths of all photoresist revenue and a materially higher share of EUV resist, where Japan is close to a monopoly and where CSET found China has nothing at all. US is DuPont, Merck's US-based EMD Electronics business and the pre-commercial metal-oxide house Inpria; the source shows no separate European column. KR is Dongjin Semichem and SK Materials Performance. The Other column is 2.4 points and is where the Chinese suppliers sit, Kempur, Nata and Jingrui, which serve mostly i-line and KrF grades; CSET put China under 5 percent of a $3.3bn photoresist market in 2019. JSR was taken private by the state-backed Japan Investment Corporation in 2024, which makes the Japanese position a policy instrument as well as a commercial one. CSET states that Japan dominates photoresist with 90 percent of the market on 2019 data, a figure on a narrower base and six years older than this one.
trend: Japan held 76.7 percent in 2021 and 78.4 in 2023 on the same measure, so the Japanese position is not eroding at the category level. Korea rose from 4.2 to 6.4 over the same two years and the unattributed Other column, where the Chinese suppliers sit, fell from 5.7 to 2.4. Chinese and Korean firms have qualified mature-node resists; EUV resist remains Japanese.

method: A CHOKEPOINTS model: no allowed source splits electronic gases by country as a category. The shares are built from the supplier set CSET lists for the segment, a $6bn market in 2019 that CSET sources to SEMI, weighted by the firms' electronic-gas businesses, and checked against the molecule-level country shares METI published in December 2025.
note: Electronic specialty and bulk gases for fabs, which is the row's weakness: it mixes the bulk industrial gases where Linde, Air Liquide and Air Products dominate with the specialty molecules where Japan and Korea do. Firm-to-country mapping: JP is Nippon Sanso Holdings/Taiyo Nippon Sanso, Resonac (formerly Showa Denko) and Kanto Denka, which lead in fluorinated etch gases. DE is Linde and Merck; Linde plc is legally domiciled in the UK and Ireland after the Praxair merger but is treated as DE here on operating-history grounds, which is a defensible but arguable call. EU-other is Air Liquide of France. US is Air Products and Entegris. KR is SK Specialty and Wonik. CN is Huate Gas, Jinhong Gas and PERIC. On the molecules that matter for etch and clean, the Japanese column understates Japan by a wide margin and the row understates China's leverage: METI, publishing Fuji Keizai's 2023 survey, puts Japan at 92 percent of fluorine gas mixtures, 97 of carbonyl sulfide, 77 of hydrogen bromide, 72 of HFC etch gases, 65 of chlorine gases and 61 of PFC etch gases, while Korea holds 47 percent of nitrogen trifluoride and China 24 percent of it and 13 percent of HFC etch gases. China also supplies most of the world's rare gases, a position that strengthened after Ukrainian neon production stopped in 2022. The least well-measured segment in the matrix: CSET names the suppliers and the market size and publishes no shares.
trend: China's share has risen since 2021 as it displaced Ukrainian and Russian rare-gas supply and moved up the value chain in fluorinated gases.

method: Node N20 in ETO's provision table: CSET's analysis of TechInsights 2025 data on a $13bn market, published in July 2026. ASML is the only supplier, so the country column is the firm column.
note: ASML is the sole supplier, on a 2025 market of about $13bn. ASML's annual report records 48 EUV systems recognized in 2025, four EXE and 44 NXE, out of 535 systems sold in units. The 100 percent figure is a vendor-headquarters number and hides the real geography: Carl Zeiss SMT (DE) makes the projection and illumination optics and is the only firm that can, Trumpf (DE) makes the CO2 drive lasers, and Cymer (US, San Diego, an ASML subsidiary) makes the light sources. A production-location cut would put roughly a third of the value in Germany. China has no EUV tool and no credible near-term path to one; its published work remains at the laser-discharge-plasma source and research-stage level. The underlying market shares are TechInsights', relayed by CSET.
trend: Unchanged at 100 percent since the technology shipped; the only movement is upward in value per tool as High-NA EXE:5200 systems enter the mix.

method: Weighted here across the three DUV nodes in ETO's provision table on their stated 2025 market sizes: ArF immersion ($11.7bn, ASML 99.3 percent, N22), ArF dry ($508m, ASML 94.4, N21) and KrF ($1.7bn, ASML 66, N105). The $13.9bn weighted total gives NL 95.1 and JP 4.9; the underlying shares are TechInsights' data analyzed by CSET.
note: Revenue-weighted across the three DUV classes in the CSET/ETO 2025 data: ArF immersion ($11.7bn, ASML 99.3 percent and 0.7 left with Japan, unattributed to a firm in the source), ArF dry ($0.51bn, ASML 94.4, Nikon 5.6) and KrF ($1.7bn, ASML 66, mostly Canon and Nikon at 34). ASML's own 2025 figures are consistent: 131 ArF immersion systems for EUR 10,311m, 16 ArF dry for EUR 427m and 78 KrF for EUR 1,001m. Excludes i-line, which is not DUV and where Canon leads with 53.7 percent; including i-line would roughly double Japan's share of the wider optical-lithography market. China's SMEE is not visible in DUV revenue; its best delivered tool remains 90 nm-class immersion-free, with a 28 nm-class ArF immersion scanner still in development.
trend: ASML's DUV share has held near 95 percent since 2021, but its China revenue mix collapsed from roughly half of system sales in 2024 as export controls and pull-forward demand unwound.

method: Node N36 in ETO's provision table: CSET's analysis of TechInsights 2025 data on a $26.2bn market, published in July 2026. The source's Swiss and British columns are grouped here into Other and its French column into EU-other; every other column is as published.
note: Covers CVD, ALD, PVD, epitaxy and electrochemical plating for front-end wafer processing. Firm-to-country mapping: US is Applied Materials, which is 41.2 points of the American column on its own, plus Lam Research at 16.9 and Veeco at 1.3; JP is Tokyo Electron (9.7) and Kokusai Electric (3.3); NL is ASM International (10.9), which leads atomic layer deposition; CN is NAURA (6.3) and Piotech (2.6); KR is Wonik IPS and Jusung; Other is mostly Swiss and UK suppliers. The shares are TechInsights' measurement, relayed by CSET.
trend: China's share has risen from roughly 1 percent in 2019 to about 10 percent, the fastest domestic-substitution gain anywhere in the equipment chain.

method: Node N55 in ETO's provision table: CSET's analysis of TechInsights 2025 data on a $29.1bn etch-and-clean market, published in July 2026. The source's 'various countries' column is carried here as Other.
note: Firm-to-country mapping: US is Lam Research (36.7 points) and Applied Materials (12.7), plus ACM Research (2.4), which is US-listed but operates chiefly through its Shanghai subsidiary and so arguably belongs partly in the CN column; JP is Tokyo Electron (22.1), SCREEN Holdings (7.8) and Hitachi High-Tech (1.7) on the clean side; CN is NAURA (5.2) and AMEC (4.4). CSIS reports Chinese tool vendors already hold about 40 percent of their own domestic etch and thin-film deposition market, which matters more than their global share. The shares are TechInsights' measurement, relayed by CSET.
trend: China's share roughly quintupled from about 2 percent in 2019 to about 10 percent, with AMEC the clearest case of a Chinese tool vendor reaching commercial parity at mature nodes.

method: Node N60 in ETO's provision table: CSET's analysis of TechInsights 2025 process-control data on a $15.7bn market, published in July 2026. The source's Hungarian column is carried here as EU-other and its 'various countries' column as Other.
note: Firm-to-country mapping: US is KLA, which at 56.8 points is over half the market on its own, plus Applied Materials (11.2) and Onto Innovation (2.6); JP is Lasertec (6.4), Hitachi High-Tech (6.2) and Rigaku (1.2); NL is ASML's YieldStar overlay and metrology line (5.9); IL is Nova (4.3) and Camtek (1.6); EU-other is Hungary; DE is Carl Zeiss AIMS mask metrology. Two chokepoints are invisible at this resolution: Lasertec holds effectively all actinic EUV mask-blank inspection, and Zeiss holds all AIMS EUV aerial-image mask review. The shares are TechInsights' measurement, relayed by CSET.
trend: The most durable US position in the chain; China remains under 1 percent globally despite domestic pushes by Skyverse and Zhongke Feice.

method: CSET's 2019 country split for photomasks, carried machine-readably as node N33 in ETO's provision table: Japan 53, the United States 40, Taiwan 7 on a roughly $4bn market, and counting captive mask shops alongside merchants. CSET built it from company financial statements.
note: The oldest figure in the matrix, and the weakest. Counting captive mask shops alongside merchants is why the US share is so high: Intel's and GlobalFoundries' in-house mask operations sit in the US column, TSMC's in TW, Samsung's in KR, and CSET found captive shops held 65 percent of the market in 2017. JP is Toppan (renamed Tekscend in 2024), Dai Nippon Printing and Hoya. What has changed since: the total market is now above $5bn, captive share has grown as leading-edge masks became harder to outsource, Photronics has added US, Taiwan and China capacity, and Hoya has become the acute chokepoint at roughly 70 percent of EUV mask blanks, a dependency that does not appear in a revenue split at all. The country columns are indicative only, and six years old.
trend: Japanese blank suppliers have strengthened at the leading edge since 2021 while merchant mask revenue shifted toward captive fabs.

method: A CHOKEPOINTS estimate. SIA and BCG measured sub-10 nm logic capacity by site in 2022 at Taiwan 69 and South Korea 31, with the United States at zero (2024 report, Exhibit 6); the row rolls that forward for TSMC's Fab 21 in Arizona, Intel's Fab 34 in Leixlip and 18A in Arizona and Oregon, and Samsung's Taylor fab.
note: The only estimate in the matrix's manufacturing rows. Capacity is counted by fab location, wherever the company is headquartered, which is the right cut for this segment because it is where the physical risk sits. TW is TSMC's Fab 18 and Fab 20 complexes in Tainan and Hsinchu. The EU-other column is Intel's Fab 34 in Leixlip, Ireland, running Intel 4 and Intel 3. JP is zero because Rapidus remains at pilot scale. China is zero at this definition; SMIC's 7 nm-class N+2 output is real but is not a 5 nm node and is produced without EUV. Nobody publishes a current measurement of this segment.
trend: Taiwan's share is falling slowly from about 69 percent as the US column goes from zero to double digits, but concentration remains the single most extreme geographic risk in the chain.

method: A CHOKEPOINTS estimate placed between two measurements: SIA and BCG's 2022 capacity split for logic at 28 nm and above (China 33, Taiwan 30, Japan 10, Other 9, US 8, Korea 5, Europe 4; 2024 report, Exhibit 6) and CSIS's finding in March 2026 that China now holds about half of global mature-node capacity on a broader definition that includes discretes, analog and power.
note: Capacity by fab location. The two measurements the row sits between are not directly comparable, because CSIS uses a broader legacy definition than SIA and BCG's logic-only one, and China is rolled forward to 38 between them. DE is split out from EU-other to capture Infineon Dresden, Bosch Reutlingen and the automotive analog base; EU-other is mostly STMicroelectronics in France and Italy. China's number carries the widest error bar in the matrix.
trend: China's share of mature logic has risen from roughly 30 percent in 2021 toward 40 percent and is the main driver of trailing-edge price deflation and of Section 232 and tariff pressure.

method: Firm shares printed in SK hynix's Form 424B4 prospectus of July 2026 (SK hynix 34.8, Samsung 34.5, Micron 23.5, Others 7.3 for 2025), summed to country by parent-company headquarters. The prospectus attributes the figures to IDC, Worldwide Memory Market Shares.
note: The figures are IDC's, adopted by SK hynix in a registered prospectus, which is a company filing with securities-law liability attached. This is revenue, and bits would give a different picture: 2025 was a price spike, so a revenue share says as much about pricing as about who can make what. It is by headquarters: Micron fabs most of its bits in Taiwan and Japan, so a production cut would move them. And 'Others' is unattributed in the source; it is the column holding CXMT, Nanya, Winbond and PSMC, and it grew from 5.1 in 2024 to 7.3 in 2025 and 9.9 in the first quarter of 2026, which is the fastest-moving number in the row.
trend: SK hynix passed Samsung for the first time in 2025 on the strength of HBM, then fell back behind it in the first quarter of 2026. The structural move is the 'Others' column, which has nearly doubled since 2024; SemiAnalysis models CXMT at 9 percent of global DRAM bit shipments in 2025 rising to 12 percent by 2027, in DDR4 and consumer parts, away from the server DDR5 and HBM that AI buyers compete for.

method: Firm shares printed in the same SK hynix Form 424B4 prospectus (SK hynix 63.2, Samsung 19.3, Micron 17.4 for 2025), summed to country by parent-company headquarters; columns sum to 99.9 because of rounding in the source. The prospectus attributes the figures to IDC.
note: There is no fourth supplier and no Chinese column at all. The prospectus's series also shows how fast the ranking moves on qualification: in 2024 the split was SK hynix 56.4, Samsung 37.8 and Micron 5.8, which is Korea at 94.2; by the first quarter of 2026 Micron was at 23.1 and Korea down to 76.9. The figures are IDC's, carried in SK hynix's registered prospectus. China has no HBM production that clears both the export-control thresholds and the performance bar, which is the binding constraint on Huawei's Ascend line and the reason Huawei designed its own HiBL and HiZQ stacks. HBM is itself a controlled item under ECCN 3A090.c, so the segment is unusual in being both extremely concentrated and directly regulated. The base die under HBM4 is now a logic die, which pulls TSMC and Samsung Foundry into a segment that used to be pure memory.
trend: Korea's share has fallen from 94.2 percent in 2024 to 82.5 in 2025 and 76.9 in the first quarter of 2026, entirely to Micron; the ranking among the three moves on qualification wins, and none of the three is Chinese.

method: No shares. No allowed source publishes 2.5D or 3D packaging capacity by country: TSMC's disclosures, SEMI, SIA and ETO's provision table carry advanced-packaging tools (node N109) and no advanced-packaging capacity.
note: The demand side is measured. Epoch AI estimates that Nvidia consumed 60.3 percent of the world's CoWoS capacity in 2025 (90 percent CI 56.5 to 64.3), Google 13.5, AMD 8.4 and Amazon 7.4, and that those four took around 90 percent of all CoWoS and all HBM by value while using about 12 percent of advanced logic die production. That is a split by buyer, and it is the sharpest published measure of how narrow the segment is. Epoch builds the estimate on year-end wafers-per-month benchmarks taken from SemiWiki and TrendForce, so the figure is relayed market research, with no institutional measurement behind it. On the supply side what is documented is dependence: Nvidia's annual report states that it uses CoWoS and names TSMC and Samsung as its foundries, and TSMC's CoWoS lines are in Taiwan; the American additions are Intel's EMIB and Foveros lines in Arizona, Oregon and New Mexico and Amkor's Arizona build, and the Korean ones are Samsung I-Cube and SK hynix's HBM stacking. The geography is overwhelmingly Taiwanese and unmeasured.
trend: Advanced packaging was the binding constraint on AI accelerator output through late 2024 and early 2025; SemiAnalysis reported in March 2026 that CoWoS had eased and front-end wafer capacity had become the dominant bottleneck. The capacity being added outside Taiwan is real but small against TSMC's base.

method: ATP site capacity by country on a $95bn market in 2022, taken from SIA and carried at stage level (S3) in ETO's provision table; SIA and BCG print the same 2022 split in their 2024 report (Exhibit 2). Columns sum to 99 because of rounding in the source.
note: Four years old, in the segment that has moved most, and there is nothing newer to move to: a search on 10 September 2026 of ETO, SIA and BCG's 2024 report, the 2025 SIA Factbook and SEMI's releases found no country split of assembly and test capacity after 2022, and the merchant OSATs file their own plant lists without the captive half of the stage that would make a denominator. It is by site, so Amkor's plants count in Korea, the Philippines, Vietnam and China and none of them in the United States, which is why the US column is 3. And it counts captive assembly and test inside IDMs and foundries alongside the merchant OSATs, which is most of what Taiwan, Korea and Japan are doing here. The 20-point 'various countries' column is not attributed in the source; SIA and BCG put Malaysia, Singapore and Vietnam at about a fifth of global assembly capacity by location, which is consistent with reading it as Southeast Asia.
trend: China has the largest single share of assembly and test capacity by site and has been adding it faster than anyone else, which is why the export controls reach packaging tools as well as wafer tools.

method: No shares. Both candidate sources name the suppliers without measuring them: every share field in ETO's Substrates node (N96) is blank, and the White House hundred-day supply chain review names the same firms and lists ABF substrate among the materials commenters flagged, again with no shares.
note: ETO's Substrates node lists Ibiden, Shinko, Nan Ya, Samsung, Shennan Circuits, Zhuhai Yueya and AKM against Japan, Korea, Taiwan and China and stops there; the White House review names the same firms the same way. The firms themselves report substrates inside broader electronics segments. The supplier set is therefore the useful part and it is stable: Unimicron, Nan Ya PCB and Kinsus in Taiwan; Ibiden and Shinko Electric Industries in Japan; Samsung Electro-Mechanics, LG Innotek, Simmtech and Daeduck in Korea; AT&S in Austria; Shennan Circuits and Zhen Ding in China. There is no US-headquartered volume supplier, which is what the 2021 review pointed out. The AI-relevant sub-segment is narrower still: the very large, high-layer-count ABF substrates that sit under CoWoS packages come from a handful of Japanese, Taiwanese and Austrian plants, and substrates are the constraint most often named after CoWoS itself. One firm-level number is on the record, from Ibiden's own investor briefing of May 2026: it says it typically takes close to 100 percent of a new generation of interposer-type substrates at launch and loses 20 to 30 points three to six months later.
trend: Chinese suppliers have grown at mature grades while Japan and Austria have held the high-layer-count ABF business that AI packages need; no allowed source measures the movement.

method: A CHOKEPOINTS estimate: no allowed source publishes AI accelerator silicon as a market with country shares. The US column is built from the design owners' filed revenue, chiefly Nvidia's $193,737m of data-center revenue in the year to January 2026 out of $215,938m total and Broadcom's $63,887m FY2025 total, of which AI silicon is a large and undisclosed slice; the Chinese column follows CSIS's work on domestic substitution.
note: Revenue of AI accelerator silicon attributed to the country of the firm that owns the design, merchant and captive combined. US is Nvidia, whose data-center revenue was $193.7bn in the year to January 2026 out of $215.9bn total, plus AMD's Instinct line, plus the custom ASIC programs that Broadcom ($63.9bn total revenue FY2025) and Marvell design for Google, Meta, OpenAI and Amazon, plus Intel Gaudi. Google TPU and AWS Trainium revenue is credited to the US because the design owner is US even though Broadcom, Alchip and MediaTek do much of the physical implementation; crediting the design-service houses instead would move a few points to TW. CN is Huawei HiSilicon Ascend, Cambricon, Biren, Moore Threads and MetaX. The Chinese column is the softest number in the row: CSIS's March 2026 piece, the basis for it, reports that domestic parts are taking a fast-growing share of China's own AI chip market, and the figure it gives for that domestic share is TrendForce's, relayed. A fast-growing share of China's market is still a small share of the world's, which is what about 5 percent globally reflects. Design location: almost all of the US column is manufactured in Taiwan.
trend: US share has stayed above 90 percent since 2021, but the internal mix has shifted from Nvidia-only toward hyperscaler ASICs designed with Broadcom, Marvell and Alchip. No allowed source publishes the merchant-versus-ASIC split.

method: No shares. AI server and rack integration shares are published only by market-research firms. CSET's brief on big tech in Taiwan, CSIS's Indo-Pacific mapping and Epoch AI's chip-owner work carry no country split for the stage, and the ODMs report consolidated revenue without breaking out AI systems.
note: Nvidia's annual report anchors what can be said: it names Hon Hai Precision Industry, Wistron and Fabrinet among the contract manufacturers that perform assembly, testing and packaging for it, states that its supply chain is currently concentrated in Asia, and says it is expanding into the United States and Latin America. That is a heavily Taiwanese ODM base whose physical assembly footprint is moving toward North America under tariff and customer pressure, with Dell, HPE and Supermicro in the American column and Inspur, Lenovo, H3C and Sugon selling into the Chinese domestic market.
trend: Headquarters and assembly location have been diverging since 2023: the Taiwanese ODMs still design and win the racks, while more of the physical integration happens in Mexico, Texas and Wisconsin.
